The letter H is never pronounced. You simply skip it.
J sounds like the English “h”, but much stronger, from the throat, like the “ch” in Scottish “loch”.
LL sounds almost like the English “y” in “yes”: me llamo = “me yamo”. In Argentina it sounds like “sh”.
A single R is a quick tap of the tongue, like the “tt” in American “butter”. R at the start of a word, or RR, is rolled 3–4 times: Rumanía, perro.
The written accent shows you exactly which syllable is stressed: a-DIÓS, per-DÓN, MÉ-di-co, Ru-ma-NÍ-a.
1. How to greet people, depending on the time
In English we have “good morning”, “good afternoon” and “good evening”. Spanish has exactly the same system, only the hours are split a little differently.
after lunch, until it gets dark (≈ 8–9 pm)
in the evening and at bedtime
“Hola” (hi) works any time and with anyone. Spaniards often combine them: “¡Hola, buenos días!”.
“Días” is masculine, so “buenOS días”. “Tardes” and “noches” are feminine, so “buenAS tardes”, “buenAS noches”. The typical mistake: “buenos tardes”.

See you! (the most common, even if you won’t see each other again today)
Pronouns are the short words that stand for a person: I, you, he… Here they all are. You don’t need to learn them perfectly today, but take a good look at the table.

Unlike English, Spanish usually does NOT say the pronoun. English says “I am Ana”; Spanish just says “Soy Ana”, because the verb already shows who it is. You add “yo” only for emphasis: “Yo soy de Madrid” = “I’M from Madrid (unlike you)”. That’s exactly what Ana does in the dialogue.

“Tú” or “usted”? “Tú” is for friends, colleagues, family, children and young people. “Usted” is for older strangers, at the bank, at the doctor’s. Spaniards use “tú” very often, much more than you might expect.
Watch the accent: “tú” (with an accent) = “you”. “tu” (without an accent) = “your”: “tu casa” = “your house”. The accent changes the meaning.
3. The verb SER = to be, step by step

SER means “to be”. As in English (I am, you are, he is…), the form changes with the person, but Spanish has a different form for every person. It is the most important verb in Spanish, so it’s worth learning by heart.
Memory trick: ES looks like English “is”, SON sounds a bit like “are” in many languages. Say them out loud 5 times: soy, eres, es, somos, sois, son.
In this chapter you use SER for three important things:
1) Who you are: I am Ana.
2) Where you are from: I am from Romania.
3) What you do for a living: I am a doctor.
For “how you feel” you do NOT use SER. “I’m fine” is “Estoy bien”, with another verb, ESTAR, which we learn in chapter 2. For now, remember the ready-made phrase: “¿Qué tal? — Muy bien, gracias.”
Watch out: in English you say “I am a doctor”, but in Spanish you say “I am doctor”, with no article.
“Soy un médico” is wrong in a simple sentence. Don’t put “un / una” in front of the job.
Many jobs have a masculine and a feminine form. The rule is simple:
To make a sentence negative, you put “no” in front of the verb. You don’t need “do / don’t” as in English. Nothing else changes.
In answers it appears twice: “No, no soy…”. The first “no” is the answer, the second is the negation (“No, I’m not…”).
Are you a student? — No, I’m not a student.
In Spanish the question mark also goes at the beginning, upside down: ¿…? That way you know from the very start that a question is coming, and you raise your voice at the end.
The same goes for exclamations: ¡Hola! ¡Qué bien!
In yes/no questions the word order does NOT change, and there is no “do” or “are you” inversion as in English. You only change the intonation: “Eres estudiante.” → “¿Eres estudiante?”
Question words always have an accent: cómo, dónde, qué. Without the accent, “como” means “like / as” or “(I) eat”.
What do you say at 4 pm?
After lunch and until it gets dark: “buenas tardes”.
Jobs are said without “un”: “Soy médico” (I am a doctor).
You politely ask an older gentleman: “Are you from Madrid?”
“Usted” (polite you) uses the 3rd person form: es.
Don’t forget the ¿ and the accent on “dónde”.
Word for word it would be “much pleasure”, but it is used as “nice to meet you”.
How do you say “See you tomorrow!”?
How are you? — Very well, thank you.
Primera clase en la escuela de idiomas
Mihai’s first day at the language school. The teacher asks the students to introduce themselves.
Today is the first day of class at a language school in Madrid.
The teacher is called Marta. She is from Toledo and she is very nice.
Marta says: “Hello, everyone! What are your names?”
The first student says: “My name is Tom. I’m from England. I’m an engineer.”
A girl says: “I’m Lena. I’m from Germany. I’m not an engineer, I’m a student.”
Then Mihai speaks: “Good afternoon. My name is Mihai and I’m from Romania. I’m a doctor.”
Marta asks: “Which city are you from, Mihai?”
“I’m from Bucharest, the capital of Romania.”
There are two classmates from Italy. They are called Giulia and Sara. They are music teachers.
There is also a boy from Japan. His name is Kenji and he is a cook.
Kenji says: “Nice to meet you. My Spanish isn’t very good.”
Marta answers: “Never mind! We’re a very international class.”
At the end, everyone says: “Goodbye! See you tomorrow!”
My name is Kenji. I’m from Japan, from Osaka.
I’m a cook. I’m not a student, but I’m learning Spanish at a school in Madrid.
My teacher is called Marta. She is from Toledo and she is very nice.
In my class there is a boy from Romania. His name is Mihai and he is a doctor.
In the morning I say: “Good morning!”. In the afternoon I say: “Good afternoon!”.
And in the evening I say: “See you tomorrow, Madrid!”.
